passages.text: Frequency-Domain Models for Nonlinear Microwave Devices Based on Large-Signal Measurements

In this paper, we introduce nonlinear large-signal scattering ( ) parameters, a new type of frequency-domain mapping that relates incident and reflected signals. <sentence_start/>We present a general form of nonlinear large-signal -parameters and show that they reduce to classic -parameters in the absence of nonlinearities. <sentence_start/>Nonlinear large-signal impedance ( ) and admittance ( ) parameters are also introduced, and equations relating the different representations are derived. <sentence_start/>We illustrate how nonlinear large-signal -parameters can be used as a tool in the design process of a nonlinear circuit, specifically a single-diode 1 GHz frequency-doubler. <sentence_start/>For the case where a nonlinear model is not readily available, we developed a method of extracting nonlinear large-signal -parameters obtained with artificial neural network models trained with multiple measurements made by a nonlinear vector network analyzer equipped with two sources. <sentence_start/>Finally, nonlinear large-signal -parameters are compared to another form of nonlinear mapping, known as nonlinear scattering functions. <sentence_start/>The nonlinear large-signal -parameters are shown to be more general.
1. <sentence_start/>Introduction

Vector network analyzers (VNAs) are one of the most versatile instruments available for RF and microwave measurements. <sentence_start/>They are used to measure complex scattering parameters (<italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters) of linear devices or circuits. <sentence_start/>RF engineers use them to verify their designs, confirm proper performance, and diagnose failures. <sentence_start/>A VNA works by exciting a linear device under test (DUT) with a series of sine wave signals, one frequency at a time, and detecting the response of the DUT at its signal ports. <sentence_start/>Since the DUT is linear, the input and output signal frequencies are the same as the source; these signals can be described by complex numbers that account for the signals’ amplitudes and phases. <sentence_start/>The input-output relationships are described by ratios of complex numbers, known as <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters. <sentence_start/>For a two-port network, four <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters completely describe the behavior of a linear DUT when excited by a sine wave at a particular frequency. <sentence_start/>Although the measurement of <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters by VNAs is invaluable to the microwave designer for modeling and measuring linear circuits, these measurements are oftentimes inadequate for nonlinear circuits operating at large-signal conditions, since nonlinearities transfer energy from the stimulus frequency to products at new frequencies. <sentence_start/>Thus, conventional linear network analysis, which relies on the assumption of superposition, must be replaced by a more general type of analysis, which we refer to as nonlinear network analysis.

Nonlinear network analysis involves characterizing a nonlinear device under realistic, large-signal operating conditions. <sentence_start/>To do this, complex traveling waves (rather than ratios) are measured at the ports of a DUT not only at the stimulus frequency (or frequencies), but also at other frequencies where energy may be created. <sentence_start/>Assuming the input signals are sine-waves and the DUT exhibits neither sub-harmonic nor chaotic behavior, the input and output signals will be combinations of sine-wave signals, caused by the nonlinearity of the DUT in conjunction with impedance mismatches between the measuring system and the DUT. <sentence_start/>If a single excitation frequency is present, new frequency components will appear at harmonics of the excitation frequency, and if multiple excitation frequencies are present, new frequency components will appear at the intermodulation products as well as at harmonics of each of the excitation frequencies. <sentence_start/>In practice, there will be a limited number of significant harmonics and intermodulation products. <sentence_start/>The set of frequencies at which energy is present and must be measured is known as the frequency grid.

A class of instruments known as nonlinear vector network analyzers (NVNA) are capable of providing accurate waveform vectors by acquiring and correcting the magnitude and phase relationships between the fundamental and harmonic components in the periodic signals [<citation rid="b1-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">1</citation>-<citation rid="b5-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">5</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An NVNA excites a nonlinear DUT with one or more sine wave signals and detects the response of the DUT at its signal ports. <sentence_start/>Assuming the DUT does not exhibit any sub-harmonic or chaotic behavior, the input and output signals will be combinations of sine wave signals due to the nonlinearity of the DUT in conjunction with mismatches between the system and the DUT. <sentence_start/>With these facts in mind, the major difference between a linear VNA and an NVNA is that a VNA measures ratios between input and output waves one frequency at a time while an NVNA measures the actual input and output waves simultaneously over a broad band of frequencies.

Even though <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters cannot adequately represent nonlinear circuits, some type of parameters relating incident and reflected signals are beneficial so that the designers can “see” application-specific engineering figures of merit that are similar to what they are accustomed to. <sentence_start/>In first part of this paper, we propose definitions of such ratios that we refer to as nonlinear large-signal scattering ( ) parameters. <sentence_start/>We also introduce nonlinear large-signal impedance ( ) and admittance ( ) parameters, and present equations relating the different representations. <sentence_start/>Next, we make two simplifications when considering the cases of a one-port network with a single-tone excitation and a two-port network with a single-tone excitation.

For existing nonlinear models, we can readily generate nonlinear large-signal -parameters by performing a harmonic balance simulation. <sentence_start/>For devices, with no model available, we can extract these parameters from artificial neural network (ANN) models that are trained with multiple frequency-domain measurements made on a nonlinear DUT with an NVNA. <sentence_start/>To illustrate applications and generation of nonlinear large-signal -parameters, we present two examples. <sentence_start/>First, we illustrate how nonlinear large-signal -parameters can be used as a tool in the process of designing a simple nonlinear circuit, specifically a single-diode 1 GHz frequency-doubler circuit. <sentence_start/>And secondly, we describe a method for generating nonlinear large-signal -parameters based upon ANN models trained on frequency-domain data measured using an NVNA. <sentence_start/>We compare a diode circuit model, generated using this method, to a harmonic balance simulation of a commercial device model.

Finally, we compare our nonlinear large-signal -parameters to another form of nonlinear mapping, known as nonlinear scattering functions [<citation rid="b6-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">6</citation>-<citation rid="b7-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we show that the two formulations are not equivalent. <sentence_start/>Nonlinear large-signal -parameters are more general than the nonlinear scattering functions, which are useful in approximating a specific class of nonlinearity in a more compact form.
2. <sentence_start/>Nonlinear Large-Signal Scattering Parameters

In this section, we introduce the concept of nonlinear large-signal scattering parameters. <sentence_start/>Like commonly used linear <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters, nonlinear large-signal scattering ( ) parameters can also be expressed as ratios of incident and reflected wave variables. <sentence_start/>However, unlike linear <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters, nonlinear large-signal -parameters depend upon the signal magnitude and must account for the harmonic content of the input and output signals since energy can be transferred to other frequencies in a nonlinear device.

After presenting the general form of nonlinear large-signal -parameters, we also introduce nonlinear large-signal impedance ( ) and admittance ( ) parameters, and present equations for relating the different representations. <sentence_start/>Next, we make two simplifications in which we consider the cases of a one-port network with a single-tone excitation and a two-port network with a single-tone excitation.

2.8 <sentence_start/>Summary of Sec. 2

In this section, we presented the general form of nonlinear large-signal -parameters. <sentence_start/>Unlike linear <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters, nonlinear large-signal -parameters depend upon the signal magnitude and must take into account the harmonic content of the input and output signals, since energy can be transferred to other frequencies in a nonlinear device. <sentence_start/>We also introduced nonlinear large-signal impedance ( ) and admittance ( ) parameters, and presented equations for relating the different representations. <sentence_start/>Next, we made two simplifications, considering the cases of a one-port network with a single-tone excitation and a two-port network with a single-tone excitation. <sentence_start/>For the one-port case with a single-tone excitation at the fundamental frequency, we showed that the equation relating and reduces to the same well-known equation for the linear case if we assume that no energy is transferred to frequency down-conversion. <sentence_start/>For the two-port case excited at port 1 by a single-tone excitation at the fundamental frequency, we extracted an input reflection coefficient , a forward transmission coefficient , and a quasi-linear output reflection coefficient .
3. <sentence_start/>Using Nonlinear Large-Signal -Parameters to Design a Diode Frequency-Doubler Circuit With a Harmonic-Balance Simulator

Resistive frequency doublers operate on the principle that a sinusoidal waveform is distorted by the nonlinear <italic toggle="yes">I</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">V</italic> characteristic of a Schottky-barrier diode [<citation rid="b9-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This distortion causes power to be generated at higher-harmonic frequencies. <sentence_start/>The design of such doublers involves separating the input and output signals by filters and determining the optimum input and output matching circuits, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

Although single-diode resistive doublers are not very efficient (analysis predicts a conversion loss of at least 9 dB [<citation rid="b10-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">10</citation>]), we chose this circuit because it is simple enough to clearly illustrate how nonlinear large-signal -parameters can be used as a design tool.

In the following sections, we describe the various steps involved in designing a single-diode 1 GHz frequency-doubler circuit. <sentence_start/>Since we are using a simulator, we can force the stimulus to consist of only |<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>|, with all other <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> terms equal to zero, where <italic toggle="yes">m</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> are positive integers such that <italic toggle="yes">m</italic> ≠ 1 and <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> ≠ 1. (In practice, this condition can never be completely realized in a measurement environment.) With only an <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub> component present, we need only consider the parameters (Eq. 52), which is a measure of the large-signal input match at the <italic toggle="yes">k</italic>th harmonic, as well as the parameter (Eq. 53), a measure of the large-signal conversion loss or gain at the <italic toggle="yes">k</italic>th harmonic, plus the quasilinear (Eq. 58) to determine the output matching network at the second harmonic. <sentence_start/>Figure 2 illustrates the setups required for determining these parameters. <sentence_start/>Determining requires a second source at port 2 at a frequency slightly offset from <italic toggle="yes">ω</italic><sub>2</sub>.

In the first step, we perform a simulation on the diode alone and use to determine the optimum bias condition for converting power from the fundamental frequency to the second harmonic. <sentence_start/>Second, we add filtering networks to separate the input and output signals, and verify their proper performance by looking at and . <sentence_start/>Third, we make use of to determine the input matching network. <sentence_start/>Fourth, with the input matching network in place, we place a second source at port 2 and find the quasi-linear value of , which allows us to determine the output matching network. <sentence_start/>Fifth, we use the optimization feature of the simulator to minimize by varying the line lengths of the input and output matching circuits. <sentence_start/>And finally, sixth, we add 4 GHz and 6 GHz filters at the output (and re-determine the proper input and output matching circuits) in order to reduce the values of and , which in turn increases the value of and cleans up the output waveform.
3.1 Diode Only

In this example, we use a compact model to simulate a commercial Schottky-barrier diode. <sentence_start/>The model includes a series resistance <italic toggle="yes">R</italic><sub>s</sub> of 14 Ω, a junction capacitance at zero voltage <italic toggle="yes">C<sub>j</sub></italic><sub>0</sub> of 0.08 pF, and a reverse saturation current <italic toggle="yes">I</italic><sub>s</sub> of 3 ×10<sup>−10</sup> A.

First, we perform a harmonic-balance simulation on the diode, sweeping the bias voltage to determine which condition gives the highest value of for <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub> = 1.0 V. <sentence_start/>Note that in all simulations we set the generator impedance <italic toggle="yes">Z</italic><sub>G</sub> and the load impedance <italic toggle="yes">Z</italic><sub>L</sub> to 50 Ω After sweeping the voltage, we determine that the optimum forward bias is +0.48 V.

4. <sentence_start/>Determining Nonlinear Large-Signal -Parameters from Artificial Neural Network Models Trained With Measurement Data

Although nonlinear large-signal -parameters can be easily determined for an existing model in a commercial harmonic balance simulator by forcing all <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>’s other than <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub> to zero, they cannot be determined directly from measurements. <sentence_start/>With currently available NVNAs, the nonlinear DUT, in conjunction with the impedance mismatches and harmonics from the system make it impossible to set all <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>’s other than <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub> (assuming port 1 excitation) to zero. <sentence_start/>In order to overcome this obstacle, we propose a method [<citation rid="b12-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">12</citation>] that makes use of multiple measurements of a DUT using a second source with isolators, as shown in Fig. <sentence_start/>5. <sentence_start/>This measurement set-up is similar to that introduced by Verspecht et al. [<citation rid="b6-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">6</citation>-<citation rid="b7-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>] to generate “nonlinear scattering functions.<sentence_start/>” <sentence_start/>As a side note, we compare and contrast the “nonlinear scattering functions” with our definitions of nonlinear large-signal scattering parameters in the Appendix.
4.1 Methodology

To illustrate our technique of generating nonlinear large-signal -parameters, let us consider the case where a DUT is excited at port 1 by a single-tone signal at frequency <italic toggle="yes">f</italic><sub>1</sub> and signal level |<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>|. <sentence_start/>Utilizing a second source, we take multiple measurements of a nonlinear circuit for different values of <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> [(<italic toggle="yes">m</italic>≠1)∧(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>≠1)]. <sentence_start/>We then use these data to develop an artificial neural network (ANN) model that maps values of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>’s to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic>’s, as shown in Fig. 6<sentence_start/>. <sentence_start/>Once the ANN model is trained and verified, the nonlinear large-signal -parameters are obtained by interpolating <italic toggle="yes">b</italic>’s from the measured results for nonzero values of <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> [(<italic toggle="yes">m</italic>≠1)∧(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>≠1)] to the desired values for <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> [(<italic toggle="yes">m</italic>≠1)∧(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>≠1)] equal to zero, as shown in Fig. <sentence_start/>7. <sentence_start/>Alternatively, other conditions may be called for, where depending on the desired application-specific figure of merit.

One popular type of ANN architecture, which is used in our work, is a feed-forward, three-layer perceptron structure (MLP3) consisting of an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer [<citation rid="b13-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The hidden layer allows for complex models of input-output relationships. <sentence_start/>ANNs learn relationships among sets of input-output data that are characteristic of the device or system under consideration. <sentence_start/>After the input vectors are presented to the input neurons and output vectors are computed, the ANN outputs are compared to the desired outputs and errors are calculated. <sentence_start/>Error derivatives are then calculated and summed for each weight until all of the training sets have been presented to the network. <sentence_start/>The error derivatives are used to update the weights for the neurons, and training continues until the errors become no greater than prescribed values. <sentence_start/>In our study, we have utilized software developed by Zhang et al. [<citation rid="b14-j94jar" ref-type="bibr" count="1">14</citation>] to construct our ANN models.

To test our method of generating nonlinear large-signal -parameters, we fabricated a wafer-level test circuit using a Schottky diode in a series configuration, as shown in Fig. 8. <sentence_start/>The two-port diode circuit was fabricated on an alumina substrate by bonding a beam-lead diode package to the gold metalization layer with silver epoxy. <sentence_start/>The diode was located in the middle of the coplanar waveguide (CPW) transmission lines, with short lines connecting the diode to probe pads at both ports. <sentence_start/>We measured the test circuit on an NVNA using an on-wafer VNA line-reflect-reflect-match (LRRM) calibration, along with signal amplitude and phase calibrations. <sentence_start/>This process places the reference plane at the tips of the wafer probes used to connect with the CPW leads.

For all measurements, the first source, located at port 1, used a sine-wave excitation of frequency 900 MHz and magnitude |<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>|≈0.178 V (−5 dBm in a 50 Ω environment) at the probe tips. <sentence_start/>The second source was connected to port 2 and used a sine-wave excitation of frequency 900 MHz and |<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>21</sub>|≈0.178 V. <sentence_start/>The diode was forward-biased to +0.2 V through the probe tips. <sentence_start/>In order to obtain the nonlinear large-signal -parameters, and , the excitation from source 1 was held constant, while the phase of source 2 was randomly changed for 500 different measurements that varied slightly in magnitude. <sentence_start/>Figure 9 plots the resulting measurements of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>21</sub> in the complex plane. <sentence_start/>The nonlinearities in the test circuit, along with impedance mismatches, created other input components at higher harmonics, as shown in Figs. 10-13 for the second and third harmonics (<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>12</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>13</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>12</sub>, and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>13</sub>). <sentence_start/>These variations in <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>ij</sub></italic> allowed us to create an ANN model that could be used to interpolate <italic toggle="yes">b</italic>’s from the measured results for nonzero values of <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> [(<italic toggle="yes">m</italic>≠1)∧(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>≠1)], as shown in Figs. 14 and 15 for <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>11</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>21</sub>, to the desired values for <italic toggle="yes">a<sub>mn</sub></italic> [(<italic toggle="yes">m</italic>≠1)∧(<italic toggle="yes">n</italic>≠1)] equal to zero, or alternatively another desired device condition.
4.2 Sensitivity Analysis of ANN Models

Data from the 500 measurements were used to develop two ANN models, one for mapping values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> (<italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>12</sub>, …, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>15</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>21</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>22</sub>, …, <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>25</sub>) to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub> (<italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>11</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>12</sub>, …, <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>15</sub>), and the other for mapping values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub> (<italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>21</sub>, <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>22</sub>, …, <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>25</sub>). <sentence_start/>We performed a sensitivity analysis to determine how many training points, testing points, and hidden neurons are required to adequately train the two ANN models. <sentence_start/>Tables 2-4 summarize the results for the first model, where we map values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub>, and Tables 5-7 summarize the results for the second model, where we map values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub>.

First, we varied the number of hidden neurons from 1 to 20. <sentence_start/>All other parameters were held constant. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the 500 measurements points were divided into 250 training points and 250 testing points, and we used the conjugate gradient method for training. <sentence_start/>Table 2 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub>, and Table 5 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Both mappings show similar trends. <sentence_start/>The average testing errors decreased with increasing numbers of hidden neurons until around 14 or 16, where the errors were minimized. <sentence_start/>For more than 16 hidden neurons, the trend reversed and the errors appeared to start increasing again. <sentence_start/>Figure 16 plots the average testing errors as a function of the number of hidden neurons for both mappings.

Next, we varied the number of training points from 5 to 250. <sentence_start/>All other parameters were held constant. <sentence_start/>The number of hidden neurons was set to 14 since we found that to be an ideal number from the previous analysis, and 250 testing points were used for verification. <sentence_start/>Table 3 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub>, and Table 6 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Once again, both mappings showed similar trends. <sentence_start/>The average testing errors decreased for an increasing number of training points. <sentence_start/>However, as more and more training points were added, diminishing returns on the testing errors were evident. <sentence_start/>Figure 17 plots the average testing errors as a function of the number of training points for both mappings.

Finally, we varied the number of testing points from 5 to 250. <sentence_start/>All other parameters were held constant. <sentence_start/>The number of hidden neurons was once again set to 14, and the same 250 training points were used for model development. <sentence_start/>Table 4 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub>, and Table 7 lists the average testing errors and correlation coefficients for the models that map <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Both mappings showed that the average testing errors varied little with the number of testing points. <sentence_start/>Figure 18 plots the average testing errors as a function of the number of testing points for both mappings.

Based on the results of our sensitivity analysis, we decided to use 250 training points and 250 testing points to train and verify the two ANN models. <sentence_start/>We chose to use 14 hidden neurons for mapping values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub> and 16 hidden neurons for mapping values from the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>2</sub> to the first five harmonics of <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>The testing error was 0.72 % for the <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>1</sub> model and 0.73 % and for the <italic toggle="yes">b</italic><sub>2</sub> model, with respective correlation coefficients of 0.99997 and 0.99992.

4.4 Summary of Sec. 4

We described a method of extracting nonlinear large-signal -parameters, using an NVNA equipped with isolators and a second source. <sentence_start/>First, we showed how multiple measurements of a nonlinear circuit could be used to train artificial neural networks. <sentence_start/>Then, we extracted the desired -parameters by interpolating the ANN models for all <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>’s equal to zero other than <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>. <sentence_start/>We checked our approach by comparing our results to a compact model simulated in commercial harmonic-balance software, and showed that the two methods agree well.

We also performed a sensitivity analysis on the ANN networks, and discovered the following: (1) The average testing error decreases for an increasing number of training points. <sentence_start/>However, as more and more training points are added, diminishing returns on the testing errors are evident. <sentence_start/>(2) As the number of hidden neurons are increased, the average testing error decreases until around 14 hidden neurons at which point more hidden neurons have no benefit and can actually lead to increases in testing error. <sentence_start/>(3) The number of testing points does not drastically affect the testing error. <sentence_start/>In fact, no more than 25 testing points are needed for the models tested.
5. <sentence_start/>Overall Summary

In this paper, we introduced nonlinear large-signal scattering parameters representing a new type of frequency-domain mapping that relates incident and reflected signals. <sentence_start/>Unlike classical <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters, nonlinear large-signal -parameters take harmonic content into account and depend on the signal magnitudes. <sentence_start/>First, we presented a general form of nonlinear large-signal -parameters and showed that they reduce to classic <italic toggle="yes">S</italic>-parameters in the absence of nonlinearities. <sentence_start/>We also introduced nonlinear large-signal impedance ( ) and admittance ( ) parameters, and presented equations that relate the different representations. <sentence_start/>Next, we considered two simplified cases of a one-port network and a two-port network, each with a single-tone excitation. <sentence_start/>For the one-port network, we showed that the equation relating and reduces to the same well-known equation for the linear case, assuming no power is transferred in the form of frequency down-conversion. <sentence_start/>For the two-port case, we extracted input reflection coefficients and forward transmission coefficients, which can be useful for designing circuits such as amplifiers and frequency multipliers. <sentence_start/>In addition, we derived a quasi-linear approximation of the output reflection coefficient under normal operating conditions. <sentence_start/>These three two-port parameters allow a designer to “see” application-specific engineering figures of merit that are similar to what he or she is accustomed to in the linear world.

Next, we illustrated how nonlinear large-signal -parameters can be used as a tool in the design process of a single-diode 1 GHz frequency-doubler. <sentence_start/>Specifically, we used to determine the input matching network, to determine the output matching network, and (for <italic toggle="yes">k</italic> = 1 to 6), and to quantify the performance of the circuit at each stage. <sentence_start/>By the final stage of the design, we had created a doubler with an overall power gain of −9.56 dB, a value not far from the maximum possible predicted value of −9 dB.

For the case where a nonlinear model is not readily available, we described a method of extracting nonlinear large-signal -parameters, using an NVNA equipped with isolators and a second source. <sentence_start/>First, we showed how multiple measurements of a nonlinear circuit could be used to train artificial neural networks. <sentence_start/>Then, we extracted the desired -parameters by interpolating the ANN models for all <italic toggle="yes">a</italic>’s equal to zero other than <italic toggle="yes">a</italic><sub>11</sub>. <sentence_start/>We checked our approach by comparing our results to a compact model simulated in commercial harmonic-balance software, and showed that the two methods agree well. <sentence_start/>We also performed a sensitivity analysis on the ANN networks, and discovered the following: (1) The average testing error decreases for an increasing number of training points. <sentence_start/>However, as more and more training points are added, diminishing returns on the testing errors are evident. <sentence_start/>(2) As the number of hidden neurons are increased, the average testing error decreases until around 14 hidden neurons, at which point more hidden neurons have no benefit and can actually lead to increases in testing error. <sentence_start/>(3) The number of testing points does not drastically affect the testing error. <sentence_start/>In fact, no more than 25 testing points are needed for the models tested.
